description: I'm a Computer Science student at Garden City University passionate about AI, machine learning, and robotics. I want to use NASA's data to build practical solutions for protecting our planet. I'm looking for teammates skilled in Python, data science, AI/ML, web development, or environmental science. Most importantly, I value curiosity, creativity, teamwork, and a shared drive to build something meaningful.
summary:
TerraGuard is a free, public web app that turns NASA’s two fire-satellite records, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), into one consistent burning calendar. It covers Ghana in full detail first, then all 16 West African countries, from 2002 to today.

The two records can’t simply be added together. VIIRS sees much finer detail, and new satellites (NOAA-20 in 2018, NOAA-21 in 2023) inflate counts with no extra fire. Added raw, Ghana’s burning appears to more than double by 2024. TerraGuard places every detection on a common grid and day, and counts each burning square once, whoever saw it. It judges years on the satellites present throughout, and estimates 2002–2011 from MODIS, with a tested error of about 20%. Harmonised, Ghana’s 2024 burning is 97% of its 2013–17 level, matching MODIS alone at 96%.

Users can search any town or ask TerraGuide, our talking on-screen guide. They see when an area usually burns and whether this month is unusual, with the reason in plain words, and can download the evidence.

This gives early-warning and emergency responders, land managers, firefighters and scientists an honest fire history they can plan with. It shows its methods and limits openly, and makes no predictions.
details:
TerraGuard is a free, public web app that turns NASA’s two fire-satellite records into one consistent burning calendar. It covers Ghana in full detail first, then all 16 West African countries, from 2002 to today.

MODIS (on Terra and Aqua, since 2000) and VIIRS (on Suomi-NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018 and NOAA-21 since 2023) can’t simply be added together. VIIRS pixels are much smaller (375 m against about 1 km), so it reports roughly ten times more detections. Each newly launched satellite also raises the counts even when there’s no extra fire.

TerraGuard harmonises the two records in a few steps:

  1. Collect. We downloaded about 61 million NASA FIRMS detections and kept the 51 million that fall inside the 16 countries.
  2. Align. Every detection is placed on a common grid (1, 2 or 5 km) and a UTC day.
  3. Count each place once. A grid square with any detection on a given day counts as one active cell-day, however many satellites saw it.
  4. Compare fairly. Each month is compared with the same month in other years. The comparison uses only the satellites present every year: Terra, Aqua and Suomi-NPP.
  5. Fill the early years. For 2002–2011, before VIIRS existed, values are estimated from MODIS with a stated range. Tested on later years, the estimates have a typical error of about 20%.
  6. Flag unusual months. A robust statistical score (median and MAD on a log scale), with a threshold tuned to about 1% false alarms, marks unusual months and explains each one in words.

On top of the calendar, users can:

  • see where it burned on an interactive map for any month;
  • compare the last 14, 30 or 60 days with the same dates in every earlier year;
  • choose any area: a region, a country, a town, a latitude and longitude, or a box they draw;
  • download the calendar, grid cells, every individual hotspot, a printable report or chart images.

TerraGuide, an animated on-screen guide, lets people type or say what they need. For example, “Tamale in March 2024” flies the map to the place, marks it, and the robot points it out.

Benefits

  • It tells the truth about trends. Added raw, Ghana’s burning appears to more than double by 2024 (243% of its 2013–17 level). Harmonised, it’s 97%, matching MODIS alone at 96%. Without harmonisation, new satellites look like new fire.
  • It explains its answers. Each flag says how big the month was, what’s typical, how many years it was compared with, and whether both sensors agree.
  • Anyone can use it. It’s free, needs no login, works on phones, and offers guided start paths, voice and plain language.
  • The evidence goes with you. Every export records its source, method, area and dates.

Intended impact

TerraGuard gives the groups NASA named for this challenge a fire history they can trust and plan with:

  • Early-warning and emergency responders: is this season already unusual?
  • Land managers: when does burning start and peak here?
  • Firefighters and fire planners: which months and places usually burn?
  • Scientists: an open, tested method with reusable data.

Ghana comes first, but the same method already covers all of West Africa, where seasonal burning affects farms, forests, air quality and health. It isn’t a live alert system and doesn’t predict fires; it shows where the present stands against two decades of history.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, HTML/CSS, SQL-style data processing.
  • Data processing: pandas, NumPy, PyArrow/Parquet, Shapely; scikit-learn (Isolation Forest, used only as a benchmark).
  • Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn.
  • Frontend: React and Vite, Leaflet maps, Recharts charts, and the browser’s built-in Web Speech API for TerraGuide’s voice.
  • Testing: pytest, with 155 automated tests.
  • Hosting: Docker, Render’s free tier, GitHub and GitHub Releases for the data bundle.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fires) and NASA POWER (rainfall); geoBoundaries, GeoNames and OpenStreetMap for boundaries, places and the base map.
  • Hardware: standard laptops. No special hardware was needed.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic's Opus 5.5) and ChatGPT (OpenAI's GPT-6) helped write the code, tests, documentation, the TerraGuide assistant and the demo slides, under our direction. The AI-made slides carry a watermark. And also we used

How it’s creative

  • A new unit. Counting places that burned rather than satellite pings turns two records that disagree into one calendar.
  • It names the trap. NASA’s own newer satellites inflate the counts. We found this and corrected it, so the extra coverage is used without creating false alarms.
  • It shows its failures. The tool reports what didn’t work, such as the Isolation Forest detector missing drops, and how each choice changes the results (7 sensitivity tests).
  • A guide you can talk to. TerraGuide makes satellite data approachable for non-specialists: say a town and watch the map fly there.
  • A landing map from real data. It replays an actual burning season and shows the fires moving south across West Africa, from about 13°N in October to about 9°N in January.

Factors our team considered

  • Honesty. Detections aren’t confirmed fires. There are no predictions and no causal claims; rainfall is shown only as context. 2002–2011 is labelled as estimated, with its error.
  • Fairness across sensors and years. History uses the steady satellite set, and each sensor can still be viewed on its own.
  • Statistical robustness. We used a median and MAD instead of a mean, calibrated the threshold to about 1% false flags, and require a minimum number of comparison years.
  • Users and access. We designed for the four NASA audiences, phone screens, reduced motion, colour-blind-safe colour scales, voice input and plain language.
  • Cost and sustainability. It runs on free hosting within 512 MB of memory, with all data published openly.
  • Scope. Ghana comes first, with full detail; the other 15 countries are covered at country level on the 5 km grid, and the site says so.
  • Rules and credit. Every data source is credited, AI use is disclosed, and there are no NASA logos.
